name: raii
intent: Tie a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime - the constructor acquires, the destructor or the language's scope-exit equivalent releases - so the resource is returned exactly once on every exit path, returns, breaks, exceptions and panics included, without any release call appearing at the points of use.
problem: Release is written far from acquisition and easy to skip: every early return, break, continue, goto and thrown exception is another exit path that can leak a file description, socket, lock, connection or allocation. try/finally-style cleanup repeats the release at each call site, is forgotten whenever a new exit path is added, and duplicates the acquisition logic that must also run before the resource can be used.
context: Code that owns a finite resource - heap block, file or socket handle, mutex, database connection, temporary file, OS handle - in a language whose semantics can bind release to a lifetime. It applies at object scope, where the owner type is the unit of correctness, and wherever an exception or early return can bypass a hand-written release; in languages without destructors the same guarantee comes from a scope-exit statement or a callback bracket, and the same trade-offs apply.
benefits: Release happens on every exit path by construction: stack unwinding, panic and early return destroy the owner, so a failure path added later cannot leak the resource.

Acquisition and release live next to each other in one type, which removes duplicated cleanup code at every call site and turns the resource's state into a checkable invariant (held or not constructed) instead of an assumption.

Exception safety becomes local: a function built only from owners gets the basic guarantee for free, and nested owners release in reverse acquisition order, which is what protocols with shared state (locks, transactions, ordered handles) require.

Ownership becomes part of the type: move semantics and delete/copy policy distinguish a unique owner, a shared owner and a borrowed reference, so lifetime errors are caught by the compiler rather than at run time.

Cleanup cost is paid once in the destructor rather than in the hot path: in C++ and Rust the owner is a value and the release inlines, so the guarantee costs no run-time dispatch compared with a handler-based finally.
tradeoffs: Implicit release cannot report failure: destructors must not throw (a second exception during unwinding terminates the process), so a failing close, flush or commit has to be surfaced by an explicit call before the owner dies or the error is lost.

Ownership must be encoded in copy/move policy: a copyable owner of a raw handle double-releases, while making the owner move-only infects signatures, containers and APIs with rvalue plumbing that a bracket helper never needs.

Release bound to owner lifetime holds the resource too long when the owner outlives the useful scope, and the guarantee is only as good as the owner's own lifetime - a leaked, forgotten or cycle-trapped owner leaks the resource too, and GC languages release non-deterministically instead of at scope exit.

Destruction order is the reverse of construction, and for statics it is fragile (statics die after main, across modules in unspecified order), which makes resources held by global owners a source of shutdown-time crashes.

In languages without the construct the ceremony is heavier than the problem: a wrapper class or a block-taking method must be written per resource kind, which is exactly the cost that scope guards and execute-around helpers exist to avoid.

participants.responsibility: The finite thing being held - heap block, file descriptor, socket, lock, database connection, temporary file or OS handle. It has an acquisition that can fail and a release that returns it to the system exactly once.

The RAII object: acquires the Resource in its constructor and establishes the invariant that this object holds a usable resource, releases it in its destructor (or scope-exit equivalent), and defines copy/move policy so ownership cannot be duplicated.

The operation that returns the Resource - deleter, close, unlock, checkin. It must be idempotent, non-throwing and tolerant of an empty handle, and the Owner invokes it exactly once when its lifetime ends.
Uses the Resource only through the Owner, cannot forget the release, and must not outlive the Owner: handles, iterators and views borrowed from the Owner are invalid once it is destroyed.
Returns a fully constructed Owner or fails without leaking anything (make_unique, open, static create), so callers never see a half-initialised owner or a public two-phase open().

use_cases: A file, stream or socket handle opened for one operation: closing in the destructor releases the descriptor on every early return and exception path.
A mutex locked for a critical section: the guard unlocks on every exit path, including exceptions and returns taken from inside the section.
A heap allocation owned by one place: smart pointers and Box keep the release with the owner, and a container of owners releases everything when it dies.
A database connection, session or transaction checked out per request: the lease is returned (or rolled back) on failure paths without each handler remembering it.
A pooled or OS-level resource (temp file, GPU buffer, file descriptor, HANDLE) that must be handed back even when the consumer fails.
The C++ standard library's std::lock_guard is a scope-bound mutex owner: construction locks the mutex and destruction unlocks it, so an exception or return cannot strand the lock.

Rust's standard library uses Drop for std::fs::File: the file descriptor is closed when the value leaves scope, while sync_all remains an explicit operation when close-time I/O errors must be observed.

Python's standard-library contextlib supplies @contextmanager and ExitStack, letting a with block compose deterministic cleanup callbacks for resources that do not expose a native context-manager type.
avoid_when: The resource must outlive every lexical scope (application-lifetime caches, singletons, connection pools): manage its lifecycle explicitly or through a container scope instead of binding release to a local owner.

Release must be owned by another component or thread than the acquirer (a pooled lease returned asynchronously, a resource destroyed on an event-loop thread): use an explicit release/return API (resource return, object pool) instead of destructor timing.
The language offers no deterministic destruction and the resource is shared: prefer a Dispose-style protocol with an explicit close or a bracket helper over hoping for collection.
Acquisition is expensive and may never be needed: acquire lazily (lazy acquisition) instead of eagerly binding the resource at construction.
Cleanup has a decision in it (commit versus rollback) that depends on the caller's intent: keep that decision explicit and let the owner guarantee only the fallback.
anti_patterns: Lapsed RAII: the owner exposes open()/close() and can exist in a half-initialised state, so callers must test and remember - the invariant the pattern exists to provide is gone.
Destructor with side effects that can fail or block: throwing, doing I/O or waiting on a lock in a destructor produces termination, deadlocks or silently lost errors.

Finalizer-based cleanup dressed up as RAII: relying on GC finalizers, __del__ or SetFinalizer to release leases, locks or connections delays release unpredictably and trades a leak for pool exhaustion.
Shallow-copyable owner: copying duplicates the handle and produces double close, double free or use-after-free; exactly one live owner must exist per resource.
Owner that releases borrowed resources: closing something it does not own (a cached or looked-up resource, or one handed in by the caller) breaks every other user of it.
design_principles: Correctness by construction: the release no longer depends on an author remembering it - the type and the compiler carry the obligation.
Single responsibility and locality of definition: one owner per resource, acquisition and release defined together, the raw resource never handed to code that could release it.
Encapsulation and information hiding: the resource handle stays private; callers see only operations that are legal while the resource is held.
Exception safety and lifetime discipline: release is the owner's job, not the error path's; the basic guarantee follows from composing owners instead of manual cleanup.
Explicit ownership semantics: unique, shared and borrowed ownership are expressed in the type, so lifetime mistakes become type errors.
best_practices: Acquire in the constructor (or a static factory returning a fully built owner) and release in the destructor; keep open()/close() out of the public API and never expose a half-constructed owner.
Make the destructor non-throwing and idempotent, and move error-observable work (flush, fsync, commit) into an explicit method that callers invoke before the owner leaves scope.
Spell out ownership in the type: delete copy operations for unique owners, implement move transfer, and use refcounted ownership only where sharing is genuinely needed.
Keep the owner's scope as narrow as the resource's use - bind it at the point of acquisition - and rely on reverse-order release for dependencies between resources.
Test the four failure paths a guard must survive: acquisition failure (no owner created), exception inside the body, early return, and an accidental double release.

Never treat finalizers, cleaners or GC hooks as the release point; if the language lacks deterministic destruction, extend the language's own bracket idiom (context manager, use, with-style helper, dispose protocol).
sources: Bjarne Stroustrup, The C++ Programming Language (4th ed., Addison-Wesley, 2013) - resource management and exception safety: resources are acquired in constructors and released in destructors; the idiom was developed for exception-safe C++ by Stroustrup and Andrew Koenig between 1984 and 1989 and the term was coined by Stroustrup.

Kent Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (Prentice Hall, 1997) - Execute Around Method (pp. 37-39), the pattern behind the alias half of the catalog row: one method owns the pair of actions around caller-supplied work.
